metadata.title: Quantitative Ability & Math Shortcut Tricks Handbook
metadata.subtitle: Complete Fast Mental Math, Arithmetic Formulas, and Past Paper Solutions for CSS, PMS, FPSC, PPSC & NTS

modules.title: Percentages & Fast Conversions
modules.description: Master percentage calculations mentally using the fraction equivalent table, split method, commutative rule, and depreciation formulas.

rules.name: Fraction to Percentage Fast Conversion Table
rules.rule: Convert standard fractions to exact percentages instantaneously to eliminate long divisions.
rules.example: What is 12.5% of 640? Instead of 0.125 × 640, compute 640 / 8 = 80.
rules.tip: Remember that 1/7 = 14.28% and 2/7 = 28.57% (digits double: 14 -> 28).

rules.name: The Commutative Percentage Trick (x% of y = y% of x)
rules.rule: Whenever calculating x% of y seems awkward, reverse the numbers: x% of y is mathematically identical to y% of x.
rules.example: Find 16% of 50. Swap it: 50% of 16 = half of 16 = 8!
rules.tip: Extremely helpful when one number is 25, 50, 75, or 20.

rules.name: The Mental Split Method (10%, 5%, 1% Building Blocks)
rules.rule: Break any percentage into 10% (move decimal 1 place left), 1% (move decimal 2 places left), and 5% (half of 10%).
rules.tip: For 98% of X, compute 100% - 2% (X - 2 × 1%).

rules.name: Annual Depreciation / Compounded Decay
rules.rule: When a value depreciates by r% annually, multiply the current value by (1 - r/100) for each year.
rules.formula: Value after n years = P × (1 - r/100)^n
rules.example: A computer worth Rs. 100,000 depreciates by 10% annually. Value after 2 years: Year 1 = 100,000 - 10,000 = 90,000; Year 2 = 90,000 - 9,000 = Rs. 81,000.
rules.tip: Do not subtract 20%! 10% depreciation for 2 years equals 19% total depreciation, leaving 81%.

rules.name: Successive Percentage Changes (Net Change Formula)
rules.rule: When a quantity changes by a% and then by b%, the net percentage change is given by the universal formula.
rules.example: If price increases by 20% and then decreases by 10%: Net = +20 - 10 + (20 × -10)/100 = 10 - 2 = +8% increase.
rules.tip: Use (+) for increases and (-) for decreases/discounts.

rules.name: Consumption Adjustment to Maintain Constant Budget
rules.rule: If price of a commodity increases by R%, consumption must decrease by a specific fraction to keep total expenditure constant.
rules.example: If petrol price increases by 25%: Reduction = [25 / (100 + 25)] × 100% = (25/125) × 100% = 20% reduction.
rules.tip: If price decreases by R%, consumption can increase by [R / (100 - R)] × 100%.

drills.question: What percent of 120 is 90? (FPSC Past Paper)
If X% of Y is 100 and Y% of Z is 200, find the relation between X and Z. (FPSC Past Paper)
The value of a computer depreciates by 10% annually. If the present value is Rs. 100,000, what will be its value after 2 years? (FPSC Past Paper)
The tank full of petrol in Haroon's motorcycle lasts for 10 days. If he starts using 25% more every day, for how many days will the tank full of petrol last? (FPSC Past Paper)
drills.shortcut: Let original daily consumption be 1 unit/day. Total petrol = 10 days × 1 unit = 10 units. New consumption = 1 + 25% = 1.25 units/day. Days = 10 / 1.25 = 10 / (5/4) = 10 × 4/5 = 8 days.

modules.title: Mental Multiplication & Squaring
modules.description: Perform lightning-fast multiplications and squaring using Vedic techniques, base methods, and algebraic identities.

rules.name: Multiplying Any Number by 11
rules.rule: Keep the outer digits identical and sum adjacent digits from right to left.
rules.formula: For ab × 11: write 'a', then (a+b), then 'b'. If (a+b) >= 10, carry over 1 to 'a'.
rules.tip: For 3 digits: 342 × 11 -> First digit 3, then (3+4)=7, then (4+2)=6, last digit 2 -> 3,762.

rules.name: Squaring Numbers Ending in 5
rules.rule: Multiply the leading number by its consecutive integer (N × (N+1)) and append 25 to the end.
rules.tip: Works for 3-digit numbers too: 115^2 -> 11 × 12 = 132 -> 13,225.

rules.name: Multiplying Numbers Near Base 100
rules.rule: Find the deviation of each number from 100. Left part = (Num1 + Dev2). Right part = (Dev1 × Dev2) in 2 digits.
rules.tip: Ensure the right-hand part always has 2 digits (e.g., 2 × 3 = 06).

rules.name: Product of Numbers with Difference of 2 (a^2 - 1)
rules.rule: When two numbers differ by 2, their product is the square of the middle number minus 1.

rules.name: Multiplication by 25, 50, and 125
rules.rule: Instead of multiplying, divide by the reciprocal fraction and add zeros.
rules.tip: Faster than standard column multiplication by a factor of four.

drills.question: What is the value of 85^2?
Find the product of 94 × 98 without pen and paper.
drills.shortcut: Deviations from 100 are -6 and -2. Left = 94 - 2 = 92. Right = (-6) × (-2) = 12 => 9,212.

drills.question: Calculate 48 × 52.

modules.title: Division & Divisibility Tests
modules.description: Quick tests to determine divisibility and rapid division tricks for competitive exams.

rules.name: Master Divisibility Test for 3 and 9
rules.rule: A number is divisible by 3 (or 9) if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3 (or 9).
rules.formula: Sum(digits) mod 3 = 0 => Divisible by 3; Sum(digits) mod 9 = 0 => Divisible by 9
rules.example: Is 48,726 divisible by 9? Sum = 4+8+7+2+6 = 27. 27 is divisible by 9, so YES.
rules.tip: 'Cast out nines': cancel out any digits that add to 9 as you go to calculate faster.

rules.name: Divisibility Test for 4 and 8
rules.rule: For 4: check only the last 2 digits. For 8: check only the last 3 digits.
rules.formula: Last 2 digits divisible by 4 => Num div by 4; Last 3 digits div by 8 => Num div by 8
rules.example: 753,824: Last 2 digits = 24 (div by 4 -> YES). Last 3 digits = 824 (824 ÷ 8 = 103 -> YES, div by 8).
rules.tip: For 8: If the hundreds digit is even, check if last 2 digits are divisible by 8. If odd, add 4 to last 2 digits.

rules.name: Alternating Sum Divisibility Test for 11
rules.rule: Take the difference between the sum of digits at odd places and sum of digits at even places. If the difference is 0 or divisible by 11, the number is divisible by 11.
rules.example: Test 9,183,724: Odd places (from right): 4+7+8+9 = 28. Even places: 2+3+1 = 6. Difference = 28 - 6 = 22 (divisible by 11 -> YES).
rules.tip: Extremely common in FPSC, CSS, and PPSC aptitude tests.

rules.name: Fast Division by 5 and 50
rules.rule: To divide by 5, double the number and shift the decimal one place left. To divide by 50, double and shift two places left.
rules.example: 342 ÷ 5: Double 342 = 684. Shift decimal -> 68.4. 1,450 ÷ 50: Double = 2,900. Shift two decimals -> 29.
rules.tip: To divide by 25: Multiply by 4 and shift two decimals left.

rules.name: Converting Recurring Decimals to Fractions
rules.rule: Pure recurring decimals have 9s in the denominator. Mixed recurring have 9s followed by 0s.
rules.tip: Number of 9s = count of repeating digits; number of 0s = count of non-repeating digits after decimal.

drills.question: Which of the following numbers is divisible by 11?
Convert the recurring decimal 0.363636... into a simplified fraction.
drills.shortcut: Two repeating digits '36' => 36 / 99 = divide top and bottom by 9 => 4/11.

modules.title: Ratio, Proportion & Variations
modules.description: Fast techniques for combining multiple ratios, finding fourth proportionals, and solving mixture replacement problems.

rules.name: The 'N-Method' to Combine Two Ratios (A:B and B:C -> A:B:C)
rules.rule: Multiply vertically and diagonally to find the unified ratio without finding common multiples.
rules.tip: Keep A:B on top and B:C on bottom aligned at B.

rules.name: Combining 4 Ratios (A:B:C:D)
rules.rule: Align ratios in a table and fill empty spaces with the adjacent number.
rules.formula: Row 1: [A, B, B, B]; Row 2: [A, B, C, C]; Row 3: [A, B, C, D] -> multiply columns.
rules.tip: Simplify the final ratio by dividing by common factors if any.

rules.name: Equivalent Ratio Property
rules.rule: Multiplying or dividing both antecedent and consequent by the same non-zero number produces an equivalent ratio.
rules.example: A ratio equivalent to 3:7 is (3×3) : (7×3) = 9:21 (FPSC Exam Question).
rules.tip: Check each option by dividing both numbers by their GCD to see if it reduces to original.

rules.name: Mixture Replacement Formula (Successive Dilution)
rules.rule: If a container has V liters of pure liquid and x liters are drawn out and replaced with water n times, the remaining pure liquid quantity is given by:
rules.example: A vessel has 40L of milk. 4L are drawn and replaced with water, repeated twice (total 2 operations). Remaining = 40 × [1 - 4/40]^2 = 40 × (0.9)^2 = 40 × 0.81 = 32.4 Liters.
rules.tip: Saves up to 3 minutes over step-by-step fractional calculation.

drills.question: A ratio equivalent to 3 : 7 is: (FPSC Past Paper)
If A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 8 : 9, find A : C.
Rs. 1,200 is divided among A, B, and C in the ratio 2 : 3 : 5. What is B's share?
drills.shortcut: Total parts = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 parts. 1 part = 1,200 / 10 = Rs. 120. B's share = 3 parts = 3 × 120 = Rs. 360.

modules.title: Work, Time & Wages
modules.description: Master individual work, team work, pipes & cisterns, and man-days formulas without cumbersome fractions.

rules.name: Two Workers Together Shortcut (Product over Sum)
rules.rule: If Person A completes work in A hours and Person B in B hours, working together they finish in (A × B) / (A + B) hours.
rules.example: Mr. A completes work in 6 hours, Mr. B in 12 hours. Together: (6 × 12) / (6 + 12) = 72 / 18 = 4 hours! (FPSC Past Paper).
rules.tip: Instant 5-second solution; avoids adding 1/6 + 1/12.

rules.name: The Universal LCM (Unit Work) Method
rules.rule: Assume total work is the LCM of the individual times. Calculate daily/hourly units of work for each person.
rules.formula: Total Units = LCM(t1, t2, t3); Combined Daily Units = u1 + u2 + u3; Time = Total Units / Combined Units
rules.example: A does work in 10 days, B in 15 days, C in 30 days. LCM = 30 units. A = 3 units/day, B = 2 units/day, C = 1 unit/day. Combined = 3+2+1 = 6 units/day. Time = 30 / 6 = 5 days.
rules.tip: Handles workers leaving early, alternate day working, and negative work (leaks) effortlessly.

rules.name: Man-Days-Hours-Work Formula (MDH / W)
rules.rule: The relation between workers, days, daily hours, efficiency, and work done across two scenarios is constant.
rules.example: If 15 men can build a 100m wall in 10 days working 8 hrs/day, how many days will 20 men take to build a 200m wall working 6 hrs/day? (15 × 10 × 8) / 100 = (20 × D2 × 6) / 200 => 12 = (120 × D2)/200 => D2 = 20 days.
rules.tip: If work is identical, simply equate M1×D1×H1 = M2×D2×H2.

rules.name: Pipes & Cisterns (Inlet and Leak Combined)
rules.rule: Inlets perform positive work; leaks/outlets perform negative work. If Inlet fills in A hours and Outlet empties in B hours (where B > A):
rules.formula: Net Time to Fill = (A × B) / (B - A)
rules.example: A pipe fills a tank in 6 hours, but a leak empties it in 10 hours. Time to fill: (6 × 10) / (10 - 6) = 60 / 4 = 15 hours.
rules.tip: If tank is emptying, time = (A × B) / (A - B).

drills.question: Mr. A can do a particular work in 6 hours, and Mr. B can do the same work in 12 hours. How much time will it take if they do the work together? (FPSC Past Paper)
12 workers can complete a project in 18 days. In how many days can 9 workers complete the same project?
Pipe A can fill a pool in 20 minutes and Pipe B can fill it in 30 minutes. If both are opened together, how long will it take?

modules.title: Time, Speed & Distance
modules.description: Solve train crossings, relative speed, average speed, and river boat problems with instant formulas.

rules.name: Instant Speed Unit Conversion (km/h <-> m/s)
rules.rule: To convert km/h to m/s multiply by 5/18. To convert m/s to km/h multiply by 18/5.
rules.example: Convert 72 km/h to m/s: 72 × (5/18) = 4 × 5 = 20 m/s. Convert 25 m/s to km/h: 25 × (18/5) = 5 × 18 = 90 km/h.
rules.tip: Notice that 18 km/h = 5 m/s, 36 km/h = 10 m/s, 54 km/h = 15 m/s, 72 km/h = 20 m/s.

rules.name: Average Speed for Equal Distance (Harmonic Mean)
rules.rule: If a journey covers equal distance at speed x and returns at speed y, the average speed is not the arithmetic average.
rules.example: A car travels from A to B at 60 km/h and returns at 40 km/h. Avg Speed = (2 × 60 × 40) / (60 + 40) = 4,800 / 100 = 48 km/h (NOT 50 km/h!).
rules.tip: For 3 equal distances: Avg Speed = 3xyz / (xy + yz + zx).

rules.name: Train Crossing Relative Speed Rules
rules.rule: Total distance is always the sum of lengths. Speeds add if traveling in opposite directions; subtract if in same direction.
rules.formula: Opposite: S_rel = S1 + S2;  Same: S_rel = |S1 - S2|;  Time = (L_train1 + L_object) / S_rel
rules.example: A 150m train at 54 km/h crosses a pole: Dist = 150m, Speed = 54 × (5/18) = 15 m/s. Time = 150 / 15 = 10 seconds.
rules.tip: For stationary objects with length (platform, bridge), Distance = Length(train) + Length(platform).

rules.name: Boats and Streams (Upstream & Downstream)
rules.rule: Let Boat speed in still water = B, Stream speed = S. Downstream D = B + S. Upstream U = B - S.
rules.formula: Boat in Still Water B = (D + U) / 2;  Stream Speed S = (D - U) / 2
rules.example: A boat moves at 14 km/h downstream and 8 km/h upstream. Boat speed = (14 + 8) / 2 = 11 km/h. Stream speed = (14 - 8) / 2 = 3 km/h.
rules.tip: D is always greater than U.

drills.question: A person travels from Lahore to Islamabad at 80 km/h and returns at 120 km/h. What is his average speed for the entire trip?
A 200m long train is running at 72 km/h. How many seconds will it take to pass an electric pole?
drills.shortcut: Speed in m/s = 72 × (5/18) = 20 m/s. Time = Distance / Speed = 200 / 20 = 10 seconds.

modules.title: Profit, Loss & Discount
modules.description: Quick calculations for markup, selling price multipliers, successive discounts, and dishonest dealer problems.

rules.name: The Multiplier Factor Method
rules.rule: Convert profit or loss into a direct multiplier to obtain Selling Price from Cost Price instantly.
rules.formula: Profit of p%: SP = CP × (1 + p/100);  Loss of l%: SP = CP × (1 - l/100)
rules.example: An item costs Rs. 450. Find SP at 20% profit: SP = 450 × 1.2 = Rs. 540. At 15% loss: SP = 450 × 0.85 = Rs. 382.5.
rules.tip: To find CP from SP: CP = SP / Multiplier.

rules.name: Successive Discounts Shortcut
rules.rule: Two successive discounts of d1% and d2% are equivalent to a single net discount.
rules.formula: Single Equivalent Discount = d1 + d2 - (d1 × d2) / 100
rules.example: Successive discounts of 20% and 10%: Net Discount = 20 + 10 - (20 × 10)/100 = 30 - 2 = 28% (NOT 30%!).
rules.tip: For three discounts: compute net of first two, then combine result with third.

rules.name: Same SP with Equal % Profit and % Loss
rules.rule: When two articles are sold at the same price—one at x% profit and the other at x% loss—there is ALWAYS an overall net loss.
rules.example: Two horses sold for Rs. 20,000 each; one at 20% gain, other at 20% loss. Net Result = Loss of (20^2 / 100)% = 400/100 = 4% loss.
rules.tip: The selling price value does not affect the percentage loss result.

rules.name: Dishonest Dealer (Cheating with Weights)
rules.rule: If a trader sells goods at cost price but uses a false weight:
rules.example: A shopkeeper sells sugar at cost price but uses 900g instead of 1kg (1000g). Error = 100g. Gain% = [100 / (1000 - 100)] × 100% = (100/900) × 100% = 11.11%.
rules.tip: True Weight - Error is the actual weight handed to the customer.

modules.title: Simple & Compound Interest
modules.description: Quick difference formulas between CI and SI, the Rule of 72, and doubling-time shortcuts.

rules.name: Difference Between CI and SI for 2 Years
rules.rule: The difference between compound interest and simple interest over 2 years at annual rate r% on principal P:
rules.tip: Saves having to calculate both CI and SI separately and subtracting.

rules.name: The Rule of 72 (Time to Double Money)
rules.rule: At r% compound interest, an investment doubles in approximately 72 / r years.
rules.example: At 8% compound interest, money doubles in 72 / 8 = 9 years. At 12%, it doubles in 72 / 12 = 6 years.
rules.tip: Rule of 114 gives tripling time; Rule of 144 gives quadrupling time.

rules.name: Doubling Time for Simple Interest
rules.rule: Under simple interest, for a sum to double, the interest earned must equal the principal (SI = P).
rules.formula: Years to Double (t) = 100 / r;  Rate to Double (r) = 100 / t
rules.example: At what SI rate will a sum double in 8 years? r = 100 / 8 = 12.5%.
rules.tip: To triple under SI: t = 200 / r. To n-fold under SI: t = (n - 1) × 100 / r.

drills.question: The difference between SI and CI on Rs. 8,000 for 2 years at 5% per annum is:
In how many years will an amount double itself under Simple Interest at 5% per annum?

modules.title: Averages & Rule of Alligation
modules.description: Solve complex mixture ratios, price blending, and changing-average problems in seconds.

rules.name: The Assumed Mean / Deviation Method
rules.rule: Pick a convenient assumed average A near the middle. Average = A + (Sum of Deviations / Count).
rules.tip: Avoids adding large multi-digit numbers.

rules.name: The Rule of Alligation (Cross Mixture Method)
rules.rule: Find the ratio in which two ingredients of different prices/qualities must be blended to produce a desired mixture price.
rules.formula: (Quantity of Cheaper) / (Quantity of Dearer) = (Dearer Price - Mean Price) / (Mean Price - Cheaper Price)
rules.example: In what ratio must rice at Rs. 60/kg be mixed with rice at Rs. 90/kg to sell at Rs. 72/kg? Cheaper = 60, Dearer = 90, Mean = 72. Cross differences: (90 - 72) = 18; (72 - 60) = 12. Ratio = 18 : 12 = 3 : 2.
rules.tip: Always place Cheaper on left, Dearer on right, Mean in center.

rules.name: New Member Joining Average Shift
rules.rule: When a new member joins an existing group of n people and increases average by x:
rules.formula: Weight/Age of New Person = Old Average + (n_new × Increase)
rules.example: Average weight of 19 students is 40 kg. With teacher included (n=20), average becomes 41 kg (+1 kg). Teacher's weight = 40 + (20 × 1) = 60 kg.
rules.tip: If average decreases by x, use: Old Average - (n_new × Decrease).

drills.question: In what ratio must a merchant mix tea worth Rs. 150/kg and Rs. 200/kg to get a blend worth Rs. 165/kg?
The average score of 10 players is 45 runs. When the captain's score is included, the average increases by 3 runs. The captain scored:
drills.shortcut: Captain's score = Old Avg + (New Count × Increase) = 45 + (11 × 3) = 45 + 33 = 78 runs.

modules.title: Arithmetic & Geometric Progressions
modules.description: Sequence formulas, n-th terms, arithmetic means, and series sums frequently tested in competitive examinations.

rules.name: Arithmetic Progression (AP) n-th Term
rules.rule: In an arithmetic progression with first term a and common difference d = (T_n - T_{n-1}):
rules.tip: Be vigilant with negative common differences.

rules.name: Arithmetic Mean (AM) Properties
rules.rule: A single AM between two numbers a and b is (a + b) / 2. The sum of n AMs between a and b is n × [(a + b) / 2].
rules.formula: Single AM = (a + b) / 2;  Sum of n AMs = n × [(a + b) / 2]
rules.example: Sum of 4 AMs between 18 and 3: 4 × [(18 + 3) / 2] = 4 × 10.5 = 42 (FPSC Past Paper). Single AM between (x-3) and (x+3) = [(x-3) + (x+3)] / 2 = 2x / 2 = x (FPSC Past Paper).
rules.tip: Sum of any number of AMs is simply n times the average of the two extremes.

rules.name: Sum of First n Natural, Even, and Odd Numbers
rules.rule: Standard closed formulas to calculate series sums in 3 seconds.
rules.formula: Natural: n(n + 1) / 2;  Even: n(n + 1);  Odd: n^2;  Squares: n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 6
rules.example: Sum of first 20 odd numbers = 20^2 = 400. Sum of first 50 natural numbers = 50 × 51 / 2 = 1,275.
rules.tip: Number of odd numbers from 1 to L is (L + 1) / 2.

modules.title: BODMAS, Inequalities & Set Theory
modules.description: Order of operations, linear inequality intervals, and three-set Venn diagram formulas.

rules.name: BODMAS Order of Operations
rules.rule: Operations must be performed strictly from left to right in order: Brackets -> Orders (Powers/Roots) -> Division & Multiplication -> Addition & Subtraction.
rules.tip: Consecutive divisions evaluate strictly from left to right: a ÷ b ÷ c = (a / b) / c = a / (b × c).

rules.name: Solving Linear Inequalities
rules.rule: When multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number, reverse the inequality sign.
rules.formula: ax + b >= c => ax >= c - b => x >= (c - b) / a (if a > 0)
rules.example: What is the solution interval of 6x - 2 >= 3x + 10? 6x - 3x >= 10 + 2 => 3x >= 12 => x >= 4. Interval = [4, ∞) (FPSC Past Paper).
rules.tip: Use square bracket [ for >= or <= and round parenthesis ( for > or <.

rules.name: Three-Set Venn Diagram Formula (Inclusion-Exclusion)
rules.rule: To find the number of elements belonging to at least one set among three overlapping categories:
rules.formula: n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - [n(A∩B) + n(B∩C) + n(A∩C)] + n(A∩B∩C)
rules.example: In a town: 45% read magazine A, 55% B, 40% C. 30% read A&B, 15% B&C, 25% A&C. 10% read all three. Percentage reading NONE: n(A∪B∪C) = 45+55+40 - (30+15+25) + 10 = 140 - 70 + 10 = 80%. None = 100% - 80% = 20%! (FPSC Past Paper).
rules.tip: Add individuals, subtract pair-wise intersections, add back the three-way intersection.

rules.name: Age Word Problem Formulation
rules.rule: Express time-shifted statements with parentheses before scaling.
rules.formula: n times age k years ago = n × (x - k);  n times age k years hence = n × (x + k)
rules.example: If Amna is x years old then 5 times Amna's age three years ago is: 5(x - 3) (FPSC Past Paper).
rules.tip: Do not write 5x - 3; the subtraction happens before the multiplication.

drills.question: What is the solution interval of the inequality 6x - 2 >= 3x + 10? (FPSC Past Paper)
If Amna is x years old, then 5 times Amna's age three years ago is: (FPSC Past Paper)
drills.shortcut: Amna's age 3 years ago was (x - 3). 5 times that age is 5(x - 3).

drills.question: In a town 45% read magazine A, 55% read magazine B, 40% read magazine C. 30% read A and B, 15% read B and C, 25% read A and C, and 10% read all three. What percentage does not read any magazine? (FPSC Past Paper)

modules.title: Geometry & Mensuration Shortcuts
modules.description: Pythagorean triples, circle ratios, cylinder/cone volume relationships, and polygon diagonal shortcuts.

rules.name: Standard Pythagorean Triples
rules.rule: Memorize base right-triangle side lengths to find hypotenuse without squaring.
rules.example: A triangle has sides 15 and 20. Divide by 5 -> (3, 4, ?). The missing side is 5 × 5 = 25.
rules.tip: Any scalar multiple of a triple is also a triple: (6, 8, 10), (9, 12, 15), etc.

rules.name: Number of Diagonals in an n-Sided Polygon
rules.rule: The total number of diagonals in a regular or irregular polygon with n vertices:
rules.example: Number of diagonals in an octagon (n = 8): [8 × (8 - 3)] / 2 = (8 × 5) / 2 = 20 diagonals.
rules.tip: A triangle (n=3) has 3×0 / 2 = 0 diagonals.

rules.name: Percentage Increase in Circle Area
rules.rule: If radius of a circle increases by r%, the area increases by [2r + (r^2 / 100)]%.
rules.example: If radius increases by 20%: Area increases by 2(20) + (400/100) = 40 + 4 = 44%.
rules.tip: Applies to squares when side increases by s%.

drills.question: How many diagonals does a regular hexagon (6 sides) have?
If the radius of a circle is doubled (increased by 100%), by what percentage does its area increase?
drills.shortcut: New Area = π(2r)^2 = 4πr^2 (4 times original). Increase = (4 - 1) × 100% = 300% increase.

modules.title: Permutations & Combinations (Counting Tricks)
modules.description: Quick handshakes formula, circular arrangements, and probability complement tricks.

rules.name: Handshakes / Match Matches Formula
rules.rule: If n persons in a room shake hands with each other exactly once, the total number of handshakes is:
rules.example: 12 people attend a meeting and each shakes hands with everyone else. Handshakes = (12 × 11) / 2 = 66.
rules.tip: Identical to round-robin tournament matches among n teams.

rules.name: The Complementary Probability Trick (At Least One)
rules.rule: Whenever asked to find the probability of 'at least one' occurrence, calculate 1 minus the probability of NONE.
rules.example: A coin is tossed 3 times. What is the probability of getting at least one Head? P(Zero heads / all tails) = (1/2)^3 = 1/8. P(At least 1 Head) = 1 - 1/8 = 7/8.
rules.tip: Reduces multiple case computations to a single fraction.

rules.name: Circular Arrangements
rules.rule: The number of ways to arrange n distinct objects around a circular table is (n - 1)!.
rules.example: In how many ways can 5 people be seated at a round table? (5 - 1)! = 4! = 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 24 ways.
rules.tip: For necklaces or garlands where clockwise/anticlockwise are identical, divide by 2: (n - 1)! / 2.

drills.question: At a conference, 10 delegates shake hands with each other once. How many total handshakes took place?
Two dice are thrown simultaneously. What is the probability of getting a sum of 7?
